title: Choose the yaw-moment model
brief: Model an asymmetric-thrust disturbance and connect it to the correct effector. Read the supplied effector map and distinguish yaw from pitch and roll.
supplied: For a separate twin-engine utility aircraft, can 8.6 kN m of usable opposing rudder/vertical-tail moment balance the yaw disturbance after losing 2.4 kN thrust at a 3.1 m lateral offset?

Positive yaw turns the nose to the right, viewed from above. The right engine loses thrust; the left engine keeps pushing, creating a positive (nose-right) disturbance. deltaT is the positive thrust loss in N and y is the positive 3.1 m distance from the centreline. The rudder must create a negative (nose-left) moment to balance it. If the left engine fails instead, both moment signs reverse. Maximum usable opposing rudder capacity is 8600 N m.
Signed disturbance, required signed rudder moment, applied signed rudder moment, net yaw moment (all N m), and remaining capacity magnitude.

Offset thrust creates yaw demand. Rudder primarily controls yaw but may couple to roll; ailerons primarily roll and can cause adverse yaw. Elevator primarily pitches. Flaps change lift/drag and pitching moment; spoilers change lift/drag and may roll; propulsion contributes forces and moments. These are dominant, not exclusive, responses.
Static yaw balance only. No proof of engine-out controllability, bank limits, transient response, or minimum control speed.
Doubling lost thrust at fixed arm doubles yaw demand and reduces margin.
Right-engine loss: disturbance +7440 N m; balancing rudder -7440 N m; net 0 N m. Capacity remaining: 8600-7440=1160 N m. Full -8600 N m would overcorrect to -1160 N m net.
Zero loss → zero demand; 2400 N loss →7440 N m; 4800 N loss →14880 N m.
Plot yaw demand against lost thrust and compare with 8600 N m capacity; identify the yaw effector and the sign/magnitude convention.

Evaluate both student expressions. For illustration, apply only the opposing moment needed for balance, capped at -8600 N m. This ideal static command assumes immediate response; it is not an actuator or flight-control model.
Retain only the nominal steady yaw-moment calculation; investigate coupling, actuator limits, and uncertainty before an claim about aircraft operation.

fields.label: Signed engine-out yaw moment (N m; use deltaT, y)
fields.help: Enter a formula using deltaT (lost thrust in N) and y (perpendicular arm in m). Nose-right is positive. Use * for multiplication; omit the equals sign.

fields.label: Signed rudder moment needed for balance (N m; use deltaT, y)
fields.help: Enter the signed moment that would make disturbance + rudder moment equal zero. Use deltaT and y, without an equals sign.

fields.label: Which control surface opposes this yaw?
fields.help: Choose the control surface that turns the nose left or right.

fields.label: Explain your answer
fields.help: Explain why the engine-out moment and balancing rudder moment have opposite signs. Distinguish the moment needed from the maximum available.

checks.message: Lost thrust 0 N at 3.1 m must give 0 N m signed nose-right disturbance.
Lost thrust 2400 N at 3.1 m must give 7440 N m signed nose-right disturbance.
Lost thrust 4800 N at 3.1 m must give 14880 N m signed nose-right disturbance.
Check which control surface primarily controls yaw. This check does not assess your written explanation.
For 0 N loss, the rudder must oppose the nose-right disturbance. Its signed balance moment must be 0 N m.
For 2400 N loss, the rudder must oppose the nose-right disturbance. Its signed balance moment must be -7440 N m.
For 4800 N loss, the rudder must oppose the nose-right disturbance. Its signed balance moment must be -14880 N m.

hints: A thrust loss off the centerline creates a moment about the CG.
Multiply force magnitude by the perpendicular lateral arm; the result is in N m.
Use deltaT*y. Rudder primarily opposes yaw; do not use elevator pitch authority as evidence for this case.

sweep.units: Lost thrust in N; yaw moment in N m.

experience.scenario: Positive yaw turns the nose to the right, viewed from above. The right engine loses thrust; the left engine keeps pushing, creating a positive (nose-right) disturbance. deltaT is the positive thrust loss in N and y is the positive 3.1 m distance from the centreline. The rudder must create a negative (nose-left) moment to balance it. If the left engine fails instead, both moment signs reverse. This is a separate twin-engine aircraft, not the trainer.
experience.task: Write two expressions: the signed engine-out disturbance and the signed rudder moment needed to balance it. Then choose the control surface and explain why the moments must oppose each other.
experience.method: Moment equals force times perpendicular distance. Use deltaT and y. For this right-engine failure, the disturbance is positive. Balance requires disturbance + rudder moment = 0. The available 8600 N m is the maximum opposing capacity, not a command to apply full rudder.
experience.investigate: Compare zero, 2400 N and 4800 N thrust loss. Record the signed rudder moment needed, then decide whether its magnitude fits within the 8600 N m opposing capacity. Read the applied moment and remaining net moment: a balanced case should have zero net moment.
experience.tools: Only this app and its calculation pad are needed.

reflection.included: The model balances signed engine-out and rudder moments, with a maximum opposing rudder capacity.
reflection.omitted: It assumes the required rudder moment appears immediately; it does not model actuator delay or the yaw rate that develops before balance.
reflection.question: If the rudder takes time to move after the engine fails, what would you need to model to determine how far the nose turns before the moments balance?
reflection.help: Use one specific detail from this investigation. Explain what you would check next and why it matters; you do not need to perform that new test here.

experience.terms: Yaw means nose-left or nose-right rotation. A moment is a turning effect: force × perpendicular distance from the centre of gravity (CG). Capacity is the maximum available; command is what is actually applied.

cases.prompt: Use the signs of the two moments and the remaining net moment to explain whether the rudder can balance this engine-out case.
cases.interpretationHint: The disturbance and balancing rudder must have opposite signs. Compare the magnitude needed with 8600 N m; zero net moment means balance.
cases.evidenceNote: Applied rudder is an ideal teaching command: only enough to balance the stated disturbance, capped at the opposing capacity. It assumes your checked model and immediate actuation. The graph compares disturbance with capacity magnitude, not signed applied rudder.
